messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 55

She is 21, a young African woman who has already learned how to stand steady in operating rooms where older colleagues still sometimes mistake her for a student. Before the disaster, she organizes her life around discipline and movement. She is single, lives alone, studies constantly, and works punishing hours as a surgeon in training, comforted by routines that make the world feel precise. In the hospital, she trusts what can be repaired: bleeding stopped, fractures set, an abdomen opened and closed with care. She believes that even in crisis, skill and speed matter.

The earthquake begins on an ordinary afternoon while she is in the surgical wing. At first she thinks a heavy trolley has struck the wall. Then the floor shifts beneath her feet with a force she has never imagined. The lights flicker, metal trays crash, and someone screams from the corridor. She remembers the sound most vividly: concrete grinding, glass breaking, alarms starting all at once. She runs toward the operating theater instead of away from it. A patient is still on the table, partially prepped, while staff shout conflicting instructions. The room lurches again. Ceiling panels fall. She sees an anesthetic machine topple and hears the low, choking cry of a nurse pinned near the doorway.

In the hours that follow, time loses its order. She helps drag patients on mattresses into the parking area. Dust coats her mouth and nostrils until she tastes grit each time she swallows. Her phone does not work. Parts of the hospital have collapsed, and the triage area forms outside among car horns, blood, and rubble. She moves from one injured body to the next, stitching, compressing, cutting away clothing, trying not to register who is alive and who is not. At one point she recognizes a porter she speaks to every morning. His chest is crushed. She kneels beside him anyway, her hands moving automatically, though another part of her already knows it is useless. By nightfall, aftershocks keep rippling under them. Every vibration makes her shoulders tense. She does not sleep.

In the weeks after, she tells herself she is lucky. She is alive, still needed, still working. Many people have lost far more. She returns to the hospital as soon as services resume in temporary structures, and at first she takes pride in functioning. But the world no longer feels solid. When a cabinet door slams, her heart jolts hard enough to hurt. If a truck passes and the ground trembles faintly, she freezes mid-step, scanning walls and exits before she realizes where she is. She begins avoiding stairwells and older buildings. She chooses seats near doors. She notices cracks in plaster everywhere.

At night the memories come without warning. Sometimes she is back in the operating room, unable to reach the patient because the floor keeps moving under her. Sometimes she wakes convinced the ceiling is falling, already halfway out of bed before she is fully conscious. She starts sleeping in scrubs because they are easiest to run in. She leaves her shoes lined up by the door. She keeps a flashlight, water bottle, and phone in the same place every night, checking them repeatedly before trying to rest. Even then she sleeps lightly, startled by wind, by pipes, by her own neighbor shifting furniture overhead.

At work, she remains outwardly capable. Her hands are steady in surgery, but only until something unexpected happens. A dropped instrument can send a flash of heat through her body. During one case, when a monitor alarm sounds in a pattern that resembles the chaos of that day, her mind blanks for a second and she cannot remember the next step of a procedure she has done many times. She recovers quickly, but afterward she locks herself in a bathroom stall, shaking and ashamed. She tells no one. She worries constantly that fear is making her unsafe, that one moment of distraction could cost someone a life.

Outside the hospital, her life grows smaller. She stops meeting friends for coffee because crowded rooms make her irritable and watchful. When her mother calls, she minimizes everything, saying only that work is busy. She does not want to hear pity in anyone’s voice, and she cannot bear being told to be grateful. Grateful feels like betrayal when she still sees the porter’s face, the pinned nurse, the patients under sheets in the parking lot. She avoids the part of the city where the hospital’s old wing still stands broken. If she has to pass nearby, she stares straight ahead and grips the steering wheel until her fingers ache.

What troubles her most is not just the fear but the change in who she feels herself to be. She used to trust her own courage. Now she feels divided: the competent young surgeon others admire, and the part of her that is always listening for the earth to move again. She is exhausted by the effort of appearing unchanged. In quiet moments, especially just before dawn, she feels a heavy guilt for surviving, for freezing inwardly when others needed her, for not having done more though she knows she worked until her body gave out. She keeps going to work, keeps tying her mask, scrubbing in, speaking calmly to patients. But beneath the practiced steadiness, she lives as if disaster is not past but waiting just below the surface.
